title: Inference Serving & Latency
scopeHtml: Scope: Batching, KV-cache management, speculative decoding, TTFT and throughput.

notes.title: The two phases and the metrics that matter
notes.html:
Two phases of every request.

  • Prefill (a.k.a. prompt processing): the whole input is pushed through the model in parallel to build the KV cache and produce the first output token. It is dominated by large matrix multiplications, so it is compute-bound. Time grows with prompt length (linearly for the dense layers, quadratically for attention).
  • Decode: tokens are generated one at a time. Every step must read all model weights and the whole KV cache from GPU memory to produce a single token, so it is memory-bandwidth-bound: the GPU's arithmetic units sit mostly idle. Time grows with the number of output tokens.

Arithmetic intensity. Decode does about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token but must load each parameter (2 bytes in fp16) once, an intensity of ~1 FLOP/byte. Modern GPUs need hundreds of FLOPs per byte to be compute-bound (e.g. ~300 for an H100). So single-stream decode uses a tiny fraction of the GPU's compute, and batching (reusing each loaded weight for many sequences) is nearly free throughput until compute or cache memory runs out.

The metrics.

Metric Meaning Mostly driven by
TTFT (time to first token) delay before output starts queueing + prefill (prompt length, caching, load)
TPOT / ITL (time per output token / inter-token latency) speed of streaming after the first token model size, memory bandwidth, batch size, cache length
E2E latency total time TTFT + TPOT × output tokens
Throughput tokens/s (or requests/s) across all users batching, hardware utilization
Goodput throughput that meets the SLO scheduling, load
p50/p95/p99 distribution of latencies queueing, long requests, noisy neighbours

Latency vs throughput. Larger batches raise total throughput (cost per token falls) but each request waits longer and shares bandwidth. SLOs decide where to sit on the curve: an interactive chat needs low TPOT (~20 to 50 ms/token, "faster than reading speed"), an offline job maximizes throughput.

Worked example. An 8B model in fp16 (16 GB of weights) on a GPU with 2 TB/s memory bandwidth: each decode step needs at least 16 GB / 2 TB/s = 8 ms, so single-stream speed ≤ ~125 tokens/s. With batch 32, the same 8 ms step emits 32 tokens: ~4,000 tokens/s total, though each user still sees ~125 tokens/s (cache reads add a bit). That is why cost per token drops sharply with batching.

Real life. A restaurant: reading the whole order slip and prepping is prefill; plating dishes one at a time is decode. Customers feel TTFT as "how long until the first dish arrives".

Tech. Network systems: latency and throughput trade off, tail latency matters more than the mean.

Interview angle. Explain prefill vs decode, which resource bounds each, and why batching helps decode but not an already compute-bound prefill.

notes.title: Batching and continuous batching
notes.html:
Why batch. See above: weights are loaded once per step regardless of how many sequences are in the batch.

Static batching. Collect N requests, run them together until all finish. Problems: the batch runs as long as the longest output, short requests finish early but their slots idle ("bubbles"), and new arrivals wait for the batch to finish.

Continuous (in-flight, iteration-level) batching. Scheduling happens at every decode step. When a sequence finishes, it leaves immediately and a waiting request joins at the next iteration, so the GPU stays full. It is the default in modern servers (vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang) and typically improves throughput several-fold over static batching.

Prefill/decode interference. A long prefill occupies the GPU and stalls decode steps of running requests, causing latency spikes ("generation stalls"). Techniques: chunked prefill (split long prompts into pieces interleaved with decode steps), and disaggregated prefill/decode (separate GPU pools for each phase, transferring the KV cache between them) to tune each independently.

Scheduling and admission control. Priority queues, max batch size/tokens, max waiting time, and rejecting or shedding load when queues exceed a bound protect p99 latency. Fair scheduling prevents a few huge requests from starving others. Reserve capacity for latency-sensitive traffic and run bulk jobs on spare capacity.

Tuning knobs. max_num_seqs, max_num_batched_tokens, GPU memory utilization fraction, chunk size, scheduling policy. Measure with realistic prompt/output length distributions, not averages.

Real life. A bus that lets passengers on and off at every stop instead of waiting for a full bus to reach the end of the line.

notes.title: KV-cache management and PagedAttention
notes.html:
The cache problem. Each request's KV cache grows by one entry per generated token; its final length is unknown at the start. Pre-allocating a contiguous block for the maximum possible length wastes memory (internal fragmentation) and leaves unusable gaps between requests (external fragmentation). Early systems wasted 60 to 80 percent of KV memory this way, limiting batch size and throughput.

PagedAttention (vLLM). Borrowing from OS virtual memory: split the cache into fixed-size blocks (e.g. 16 tokens) allocated on demand and tracked in a per-request block table. The attention kernel reads through the table, so blocks need not be contiguous. Benefits: near-zero fragmentation (waste < ~4 percent), larger effective batches (2 to 4x throughput gains reported), and sharing.

Sharing and prefix caching. Requests with the same prefix (system prompt, few-shot examples, a shared document, earlier conversation turns) can point to the same physical blocks (copy-on-write). Automatic prefix caching hashes blocks so a later request with an identical prefix skips recomputing prefill for that portion: lower TTFT and compute. Parallel sampling and beam search also share prompt blocks.

Eviction and preemption. When memory runs out the scheduler can evict cached prefixes (LRU), swap blocks to CPU memory, or recompute later (preempt a request). Poor policies cause thrashing; monitor cache hit rate and preemption counts.

Reducing cache size. GQA/MQA/MLA models, KV-cache quantization (fp8/int8), sliding-window attention, and limiting context length. Cache offloading to CPU/NVMe (e.g. LMCache-style) extends capacity at the cost of transfer latency.

API-level prompt caching. Hosted APIs expose the same idea: mark a stable prefix; reads are billed at a fraction of normal input price and are faster, as long as the prefix matches exactly and is requested again within the TTL.

Real life. A hotel that assigns rooms as guests arrive rather than reserving a whole floor for each booking; guests of the same group share a lounge.

notes.title: Speculative decoding
notes.html:
Idea. Decode is memory-bound, so verifying several tokens costs almost the same as generating one. Use a small, fast draft model (or the main model's own extra heads) to propose γ tokens (e.g. 4 to 8), then run the large target model once over all of them in parallel and accept the longest prefix that the target would have produced. With the standard rejection-sampling acceptance rule the output distribution is identical to the target's.

Expected speed-up. If the average acceptance per round is a tokens (including the one the target contributes), you get ~a tokens for the cost of one target step plus the draft cost. Typical speedups: 1.5 to 3x. Gains depend on the acceptance rate: high for predictable text (code, boilerplate, summaries of given text), lower for creative text; low acceptance wastes the draft's compute.

Variants.

  • Separate draft model (small model of the same family).
  • Self-speculative / Medusa / EAGLE: extra prediction heads or a lightweight draft layer on the target model, no second model to manage.
  • Prompt lookup / n-gram speculation: propose tokens copied from the prompt (great for editing, extraction, RAG answers).
  • Lookahead decoding and tree-based verification of several candidate continuations.

When it helps / hurts. Best at low-to-medium batch sizes where decode is memory-bound and latency matters. At very large batch sizes the GPU is already busy (compute-bound), so the extra verification work can reduce throughput.

Real life. A junior writes a draft paragraph; the senior reviews it in one read and corrects only the wrong parts, faster than writing it all from scratch.

notes.title: Streaming and perceived latency
notes.html:
Why stream. Users perceive responsiveness by the time to the first visible words and by a steady flow, not by total time. Streaming tokens as they are generated cuts perceived wait dramatically even though E2E time is unchanged. Streaming is also essential for long outputs and for showing partial reasoning/progress.

Techniques to lower TTFT. Shorter prompts; prompt/prefix caching; avoid long system prompts; warm instances (no cold starts); route to nearby regions; keep queues short (autoscale on queue depth); chunked prefill; smaller model for first-line responses; speculative "typing" UI.

Engineering the stream.

  • Use server-sent events or WebSockets; flush per token or small groups of tokens.
  • Handle backpressure and slow clients (buffer limits).
  • Handle dropped connections: allow resume/retry; never persist a partial answer as complete.
  • Send metadata events (usage, stop reason, tool calls) at the end.
  • Be careful with moderation/validation of streamed content: either filter incrementally or hold back sensitive segments.
  • Proxies and CDNs may buffer responses; disable buffering for streams.

Real life. Watching the pizza being made through a window feels faster than waiting blind for the box.

notes.title: Capacity planning for serving
notes.html:
Method.

  1. Workload model. Requests per second (average and peak), input and output token distributions (not just averages: p50/p95), concurrency, prefix-sharing potential.
  2. SLOs. TTFT p95, TPOT p95, availability, max queue time.
  3. Memory fit. Weights + KV cache for target concurrency + overhead (10 to 20 percent). Choose precision/quantization and tensor-parallel degree accordingly.
  4. Throughput per replica. Benchmark the real engine with realistic traffic: tokens/s at the SLO. Tools: vLLM benchmarks, genai-perf, custom load generators with recorded traces.
  5. Replica count. required_tokens_per_s / per_replica_tokens_per_s × (1 + headroom), plus redundancy (N+1 or N+2 across zones).
  6. Autoscaling. Scale on queue length, GPU utilization and KV-cache usage, with warm pools since model loading takes minutes. Over-provision for spikes or shed/queue low-priority traffic.
  7. Failure handling. Health checks, graceful drain, retries with idempotency, fallback to a smaller model or a hosted API when saturated.

Worked example. Traffic: 20 requests/s peak, 1,500 input + 400 output tokens each. Output: 8,000 tokens/s. Input prefill: 30,000 tokens/s. If one replica sustains ~2,500 output tokens/s and handles prefill for the mix within SLO, you need ~3.2 → 4 replicas, plus 1 for redundancy = 5, with GPU memory checked for ~80 concurrent sequences × ~2 k tokens of cache.

Parallelism choices. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across GPUs (lower latency, needs fast interconnect, within a node); pipeline parallelism splits layers across nodes (higher throughput, adds latency); expert parallelism for MoE; data parallelism (replicas) for scale.

Real life. Staffing a call centre from peak-hour call volume and call duration, with spare agents, not from the daily average.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Phases and metrics. Prefill is compute-bound and sets TTFT; decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and sets tokens per second. Track TTFT, TPOT, E2E, throughput, goodput and tail percentiles. Decode intensity is ~1 FLOP/byte, so batching raises throughput almost for free until cache memory or compute runs out.

Batching. Static batching wastes capacity; continuous (iteration-level) batching keeps the GPU full by swapping finished requests for new ones each step. Long prefills disturb decode: chunk them or disaggregate prefill and decode. Admission control and priority queues protect p99.

Memory. PagedAttention stores the KV cache in blocks allocated on demand, cutting fragmentation and enabling prefix sharing and copy-on-write; automatic prefix caching reuses computed prefixes. Reduce cache with GQA/MLA, FP8 cache, windows, and offloading.

Speculative decoding. A draft proposes several tokens; the target verifies them in one pass with an identical output distribution. Speed-up 1.5 to 3x depending on acceptance rate; best at low batch sizes; variants include Medusa/EAGLE and prompt lookup.

Streaming. Improves perceived latency; reduce TTFT with caching, short prompts, warm instances; handle backpressure and dropped connections; avoid proxy buffering.

Capacity planning. Model the workload with distributions, check memory fit, benchmark real throughput at the SLO, size replicas with headroom and redundancy, autoscale on queue depth with warm pools, and keep fallbacks.

Interview one-liners.

  • "Prefill is compute-bound, decode is bandwidth-bound; batching exploits the gap."
  • "Continuous batching and PagedAttention are why modern servers get several times the throughput of naive ones."
  • "Speculative decoding is lossless: the target model verifies the draft."
  • "Plan capacity from percentiles and SLOs, not averages."

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through what happens inside an LLM server between receiving a prompt and returning the last token. Why do people say prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every serving optimization (batching, chunked prefill, speculative decoding, disaggregation) is a consequence of this asymmetry. If you cannot explain it, you cannot reason about any of them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An LLM is a program that predicts one token at a time. Prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass, builds the KV cache (saved attention keys and values for each token so they are not recomputed) and yields the first output token. Decode then generates one token per step, and each step must stream all the model weights plus the KV cache from GPU memory to produce a single token. Prefill does huge matrix multiplications, so the arithmetic units are the limit (compute-bound). Decode does very little math per byte loaded, so memory bandwidth is the limit (memory-bound).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Terms: a token is a word piece (about 0.75 English words). FLOPs are floating-point operations (the math). Memory bandwidth is how many bytes per second the GPU can read from its memory (HBM).

prompt (1,500 tokens) --> [PREFILL: one big parallel pass] --> KV cache + token 1
                                                                |
token 1 --> [DECODE step] --> token 2 --> [DECODE step] --> token 3 ... (one at a time)

Arithmetic intensity is FLOPs per byte moved. In decode, each parameter does roughly 2 FLOPs (a multiply and an add) and is loaded once as 2 bytes (fp16): about 1 FLOP/byte. An H100-class GPU can do hundreds of FLOPs per byte moved before the math units saturate, so at batch size 1 the compute units are mostly idle and speed is set by bandwidth. In prefill, 1,500 tokens reuse the same loaded weights, so intensity is ~1,500x higher and the GPU is genuinely busy.

Rough floor for decode time per step = (weight bytes + KV bytes read) / bandwidth. An 8B model in fp16 is 16 GB; at 2 TB/s that is 8 ms per step, so ~125 tokens/s per stream at best. Prefill time grows with prompt length (linearly for dense layers, quadratically for attention); decode time grows with the number of output tokens and slightly with cache length.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
(decode speed ceiling from bandwidth)

def max_tokens_per_s(params_b: float, bytes_per_param: float, bw_tb_s: float) -> float:
    weight_bytes = params_b * 1e9 * bytes_per_param
    return bw_tb_s * 1e12 / weight_bytes   # ignores KV reads, so an upper bound

print(max_tokens_per_s(8, 2, 2.0))   # ~125 tokens/s for an 8B fp16 model at 2 TB/s
fun maxTokensPerS(paramsB: Double, bytesPerParam: Double, bwTbS: Double): Double =
    bwTbS * 1e12 / (paramsB * 1e9 * bytesPerParam) // upper bound, ignores KV reads

fun main() = println(maxTokensPerS(8.0, 2.0, 2.0)) // ~125.0
public class DecodeCeiling {
    static double maxTokensPerS(double paramsB, double bytesPerParam, double bwTbS) {
        return bwTbS * 1e12 / (paramsB * 1e9 * bytesPerParam); // upper bound
    }
    public static void main(String[] a) { System.out.println(maxTokensPerS(8, 2, 2.0)); } // ~125.0
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "decode is slow because it is sequential" without naming the bandwidth limit.
  • Forgetting the KV cache read, which grows with context and also costs bandwidth.
  • Assuming a faster GPU (more FLOPs) speeds up decode; bandwidth is what matters.
  • Treating prefill and decode as one workload when tuning.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does quantizing weights to int4 speed up decode? → Fewer bytes to load per step, and decode is bandwidth-bound; prefill gains less.
  2. Why is attention in prefill quadratic? → Every token attends to every earlier token, so n^2 pairs.
  3. Where does a long prompt hurt more, TTFT or TPOT? → Mainly TTFT (prefill), though a long cache also slows each decode step a little.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "prefill processes the prompt, decode generates tokens." Senior: gives intensity numbers, computes the bandwidth ceiling, and links the asymmetry to batching, chunked prefill and disaggregation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team bought GPUs with more FLOPs but the same bandwidth and saw no chat speedup; the bottleneck was HBM bandwidth.

questions.promptHtml: Define TTFT, TPOT (inter-token latency), E2E latency, throughput and goodput. Which would you put in an SLO for a chat product versus an overnight summarization job?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows whether you measure the right thing. Averages and a single "latency" number hide the problems users feel.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: TTFT is the wait until the first token appears; TPOT is the gap between later tokens (streaming speed); E2E is TTFT plus TPOT times output tokens. Throughput is total tokens per second across all users; goodput is the part of that throughput that met the SLO. A chat product sets percentile SLOs on TTFT and TPOT (for example p95 TTFT under 1 s, TPOT under 50 ms); an overnight job only cares about throughput and cost.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
An SLO (service level objective) is a measurable target, e.g. "95 percent of requests have TTFT under 1 s". A percentile p95 means 95 percent of requests are faster than that value; tails matter because one slow request in twenty is a visible failure for a busy user.

Metric Driven mostly by
TTFT queue wait + prefill (prompt length, cache hits, load)
TPOT / ITL model size, memory bandwidth, batch size, cache length
E2E TTFT + TPOT x output tokens
Throughput batching, hardware utilization
Goodput scheduling, load, SLO strictness

Throughput alone is misleading: a server can post huge tokens/s by running giant batches while every user waits 10 s. Goodput fixes that by counting only work that met the SLO. Reading speed is roughly 5 to 10 tokens/s, so TPOT beyond ~50 to 100 ms is rarely felt in chat, but TTFT above ~1 to 2 s is.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: n/a (definitions; measurement code appears in the streaming questions).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Quoting the mean instead of p95/p99.
  • Measuring E2E only and not splitting TTFT from TPOT, so you cannot tell queueing from slow decode.
  • Benchmarking with identical prompts (cache hits) or average lengths instead of a real distribution.
  • Calling peak throughput "capacity" without an SLO.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A job emits 2,000 tokens; TPOT is 30 ms and TTFT 0.8 s. E2E? → 0.8 + 2000 x 0.03 = 60.8 s.
  2. Why can raising batch size hurt p99? → Each step is slower (shared bandwidth, more compute) and queued requests wait longer.
  3. How do you compute goodput? → Count only requests (or their tokens) meeting both TTFT and TPOT targets, divided by wall time.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "latency and tokens per second." Senior: separates TTFT/TPOT, insists on percentiles under realistic length distributions, and optimizes goodput.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dashboard showed 3,000 tokens/s and green, while p99 TTFT was 12 s because long prompts queued behind each other.

questions.promptHtml: Why does serving 32 requests at once cost barely more per step than serving one? Where does that free lunch end?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the core economic fact of LLM serving and the reason inference providers can charge what they do.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In decode, each step loads all weights from GPU memory to make one token. If 32 requests share that step, the same loaded weights are used 32 times, so the step takes about as long but emits 32 tokens. The free lunch ends when the math units saturate (compute-bound) or when the KV cache for all those requests no longer fits in memory or its reads dominate bandwidth.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A batch is a group of sequences processed together in one forward pass. Worked example: 8B fp16 model (16 GB) on 2 TB/s: one step is at least 8 ms. Batch 1 gives ~125 tokens/s total. Batch 32 gives ~32 x 125 = 4,000 tokens/s total, while each user still sees ~125 tokens/s (a bit less since cache reads add up). Cost per token falls about 32x.

Limits:

  1. Compute roof. Intensity grows with batch size (about batch FLOPs per weight byte); around a few hundred it saturates an H100-class GPU and step time starts growing with batch.
  2. KV memory. Each sequence owns a cache; total cache bytes = sequences x tokens x bytes per token. Memory caps concurrency.
  3. KV bandwidth. The cache is not shared between sequences, so its read cost scales with batch (weights do not). Long contexts erode the benefit.
  4. Latency. Bigger batches mean longer steps and longer queue waits.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: n/a (arithmetic shown above).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking batching speeds up one request; it raises total throughput, per-user speed is flat or slightly worse.
  • Ignoring KV cache growth when sizing batches.
  • Assuming linear scaling forever.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does batching help prefill as much? → Much less; prefill already uses the GPU's compute, so extra requests mostly add latency.
  2. What caps batch size in practice? → KV-cache memory first for long contexts, scheduler token budgets, then compute.
  3. How is cost per token affected? → Falls roughly with batch size until the compute roof, then flattens.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "bigger batches are more efficient." Senior: explains weight reuse, gives the numeric example and the four limits, and ties it to SLO tuning.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A replica ran at batch 4 off-peak and cost 8x more per token than at peak; moving bulk jobs onto spare capacity cut the bill.

questions.promptHtml: What is continuous (in-flight) batching and why is it better than static batching?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the baseline feature of vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM and SGLang; not knowing it signals no serving experience.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Static batching groups N requests and runs them until the slowest one finishes, so finished requests leave idle slots and new arrivals wait. Continuous batching makes the scheduling decision every decode step: a finished sequence leaves immediately and a waiting request joins at the next iteration. The GPU stays full and queue time drops, usually giving several times the throughput.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Output lengths vary wildly (a 10-token answer next to a 1,000-token one). With static batching of 8 requests, if seven finish at step 50 and one runs to step 1,000, seven slots idle for 950 steps (a "bubble"), and anyone arriving waits for the whole batch.

Static:      [A....][B........][C..]  all wait for B, slots idle after A, C end
Continuous:  [A....][D......][E.....]   slot freed by A taken by D at the next step
             [B........][F..][G..]      slot freed by F taken by G ...

Implementation: the scheduler keeps a running set and a waiting queue; each iteration it removes finished sequences, admits waiting ones if there is KV memory and token budget, runs one forward pass (prefill tokens of new requests plus one decode token per running one), and repeats. This needs a KV cache that allocates per sequence on demand (see PagedAttention).

sections.label: Code
sections.html: n/a (scheduler internals; configured via engine flags such as max number of sequences and batched tokens).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Describing it as "dynamic batching" that only waits a few ms to group requests; that still runs to completion.
  • Forgetting new requests' prefill still competes with running decodes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What knobs matter? → Max concurrent sequences, max batched tokens per step, memory fraction, scheduling policy.
  2. What new problem does it create? → Prefill/decode interference (long prefills stall running requests).
  3. Does it change outputs? → No; each sequence is computed independently (up to floating-point noise).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "requests join as others finish." Senior: explains the bubble, iteration-level scheduling, the dependency on paged KV memory, and the interference trade-off.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Moving from a naive static-batch server to a continuous-batching engine on the same GPUs let a team drop from 12 to 4 replicas at the same SLO.

questions.promptHtml: What is the KV cache, and how do you compute how much GPU memory it needs? Why does it limit concurrency more than model size does at long contexts?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Memory fit is the first question in capacity planning. Candidates who can do this arithmetic stand out.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Attention needs the key and value vectors of every earlier token. Instead of recomputing them at each step, the server stores them: that is the KV cache. Bytes per token = 2 (K and V) x layers x KV heads x head dim x bytes per value. It grows with each request's length, so total cache = concurrent sequences x tokens x bytes per token, which can exceed the weights at long contexts.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example, a Llama-3-8B-style model: 32 layers, 8 KV heads (grouped-query attention, GQA, where many query heads share fewer KV heads), head dim 128, fp16 (2 bytes): 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB per token. A 4,096-token request needs 512 MiB; 100 concurrent such requests need 50 GiB, more than the 16 GB of weights. Without GQA (32 KV heads) it would be 4x larger. (Check the actual config of your model.)

Ways to shrink: GQA/MQA/MLA architectures, fp8 or int8 KV quantization (2x vs fp16), sliding-window attention, shorter max context, prefix sharing, offloading to CPU memory.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def kv_bytes_per_token(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, dtype_bytes=2):
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes

b = kv_bytes_per_token(32, 8, 128)           # 131072 bytes
print(b / 1024, "KiB/token;", b * 4096 / 2**20, "MiB per 4k request")
fun kvBytesPerToken(layers: Int, kvHeads: Int, headDim: Int, dtypeBytes: Int = 2): Long =
    2L * layers * kvHeads * headDim * dtypeBytes

fun main() {
    val b = kvBytesPerToken(32, 8, 128)               // 131072
    println("${b / 1024} KiB/token, ${b * 4096 / (1 shl 20)} MiB per 4k request")
}
public class KvSize {
    static long kvBytesPerToken(int layers, int kvHeads, int headDim, int dtypeBytes) {
        return 2L * layers * kvHeads * headDim * dtypeBytes;
    }
    public static void main(String[] a) {
        long b = kvBytesPerToken(32, 8, 128, 2);       // 131072
        System.out.println(b / 1024 + " KiB/token, " + b * 4096 / (1 << 20) + " MiB per 4k request");
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using attention heads instead of KV heads (overestimates 4x for GQA).
  • Forgetting the factor 2 (K and V) or the dtype size.
  • Sizing for average length when the p99 length decides OOM.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does fp8 KV cost? → Slight accuracy risk (validate on your evals) for 2x capacity.
  2. Does KV size depend on batch? → Linear in sequences and tokens.
  3. Why not store only the hidden state and recompute? → Recompute is far more FLOPs per step; the cache trades memory for compute.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "cache of past keys and values." Senior: computes bytes per token from the model config, knows GQA effects, and sizes concurrency from the memory left after weights.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 128k-context rollout cut concurrency from ~100 to ~3 per GPU because nobody did this arithmetic.

questions.promptHtml: What problem does PagedAttention solve, and how does it work?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the signature idea behind vLLM and shows whether you understand memory management, not just model code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A request's output length is unknown up front. Reserving a contiguous maximum-length KV buffer per request wastes huge memory through fragmentation (unused reserved space and unusable gaps). PagedAttention borrows OS virtual memory: the cache is split into small fixed-size blocks (say 16 tokens) allocated on demand and mapped through a per-request block table, so memory need not be contiguous. Waste drops to a few percent, so batches grow and throughput rises, and blocks can be shared.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Terms: internal fragmentation is reserved-but-unused space inside an allocation; external fragmentation is free space too scattered to use.

Request A block table: [logical 0 -> phys 7][1 -> phys 2][2 -> phys 9]
Request B block table: [0 -> phys 4][1 -> phys 1]
Physical pool: blocks 0..N, any free block can serve any request.

The attention kernel looks up each logical block's physical location, so reading is slightly less contiguous but the memory savings pay for it. Early systems wasted 60 to 80 percent of KV memory; paging brings waste below ~4 percent (vLLM paper figures; verify for your version). Sharing: two sequences with an identical prefix point to the same physical blocks with reference counts; writing triggers copy-on-write. This powers parallel sampling, beam search and prefix caching.

questions.promptHtml: How does automatic prefix caching work, and what makes a workload benefit or not?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the cheapest TTFT and cost win for chat, RAG and agents with large system prompts, and it is easy to defeat by accident.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If a new request starts with tokens already processed recently (system prompt, few-shot examples, earlier chat turns), the server can reuse their stored KV blocks and skip prefill for that part. Blocks are identified by a hash of their tokens and everything before them. It only works for an exact token-for-token prefix, so anything variable (a timestamp, a user name) near the start destroys the hit.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each KV block's hash chains the previous block's hash plus its own tokens, so a block is reusable only if the entire prefix before it matches. A hit means those tokens need no prefill compute: TTFT falls and GPU time frees up. Cached blocks are evicted (typically LRU) when memory is needed.

Good fit: long shared system prompts, multi-turn chat (the history is the prefix of the next turn), RAG with fixed instructions, agents re-sending tool definitions. Poor fit: unique documents per request, prefix that changes each time, tiny prompts. Hosted APIs expose the same idea as prompt caching: mark the stable prefix, reads are cheaper and faster, within a TTL and only on exact match.

Design rule: static content first (instructions, tools, examples), dynamic content last (user question, retrieved chunks, timestamps).

• Putting the current time or request ID in the system prompt.
  • Reordering tool definitions or JSON key order between calls.
  • Expecting hits across different model versions or tokenizers.
  • Not tracking hit rate.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why exact match only? → Each token's KV depends on all earlier tokens (causal attention), so a changed early token changes every later KV.
  2. Does it change outputs? → No, apart from negligible numeric differences.
  3. Multi-replica deployments? → Hits require the request to land on a replica holding the blocks; use prefix-aware (sticky) routing.

questions.promptHtml: Why can one long prompt make everyone else's streaming stutter in a continuous-batching server, and what are the fixes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of mixed workloads and tail latency, the practical limit of continuous batching.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each engine step processes the prefill tokens of newly admitted requests together with one decode token per running request. A 32k-token prefill makes that step take hundreds of milliseconds, so every running stream waits that long for its next token: a stall in TPOT. Chunked prefill splits the long prompt into pieces (say 512 to 2,048 tokens) and interleaves them with decode steps under a per-step token budget. Disaggregation goes further by using separate GPUs for prefill and decode.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A step has a token budget (max batched tokens). Without chunking, a request with 32k prompt tokens consumes the whole step (and must fit in the budget or be given an exception). With chunking, each step takes all running decode tokens first, then fills the remaining budget with prefill chunks. Result: smooth TPOT for running users, slightly higher TTFT for the long prompt (it needs many steps), and better overall utilization because small decode batches get compute-heavy prefill work added "for free".

Tuning: smaller chunks smooth TPOT but lengthen TTFT of long prompts and add overhead; larger chunks do the reverse. Prioritize decode tokens in the budget for latency-sensitive traffic.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Fixing the symptom by lowering batch size, which kills throughput.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Cost of chunking? → Re-reading the KV of earlier chunks each time plus kernel launch overhead; a small penalty.
  2. Why not only disaggregate? → It needs fast KV transfer and more complex ops; chunking is simpler.
  3. How to detect stalls? → Histogram of inter-token latency, not mean TPOT.

questions.promptHtml: Explain speculative decoding. Why is it called lossless, and where does the speed-up come from?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the main latency optimization at low concurrency and is often misunderstood as "just use a smaller model".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A small fast draft model guesses the next few tokens (say 4). The big target model then checks all of them in one parallel forward pass and keeps the longest correct prefix, plus one token of its own. Since decode is memory-bound, checking 5 positions costs about the same as generating 1, so you often get 2 to 3 tokens per target pass. A rejection-sampling rule makes the final output distribution exactly the target model's, so quality is unchanged.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Terms: draft model (small, same tokenizer), target model (the one whose quality you want), acceptance rate alpha (chance a drafted token is accepted).

Procedure per round: draft proposes gamma tokens; the target scores all gamma+1 positions in one pass; accept token i with probability min(1, p_target/p_draft); at the first rejection, resample from an adjusted distribution; if all accepted, take a bonus token from the target. Expected tokens per round with i.i.d. acceptance alpha is (1 - alpha^(gamma+1)) / (1 - alpha).

Speed-up = expected tokens / (1 + gamma x c), where c = draft cost / target cost. Example: alpha 0.8, gamma 4, c 0.1: tokens = 3.36; cost 1.4; speed-up about 2.4x. Variants: Medusa/EAGLE heads on the target, n-gram/prompt-lookup drafting (good for extraction and editing).

• Claiming it degrades quality.
  • Forgetting the draft and target must share a tokenizer/vocabulary.
  • Assuming a fixed speed-up regardless of content.

1. When is acceptance high? → Predictable text: code, boilerplate, copying from the prompt.
  2. Greedy vs sampling? → Both supported; with temperature 0 acceptance is exact-match.
  3. Memory cost? → Draft weights and its own KV cache.

questions.promptHtml: How would you stream tokens from an LLM server to a browser or Android client reliably? What breaks in production?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Streaming is the biggest perceived-latency lever and has many non-obvious infrastructure pitfalls.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use server-sent events (SSE), a long-lived HTTP response that pushes small text events, or WebSockets. Send each token or small group as it is generated, flush immediately, finish with a final event carrying usage and stop reason. Pitfalls: proxies and CDNs that buffer the response, slow clients causing backpressure, dropped connections leaving partial answers, and moderation that only sees full text.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Streaming does not change E2E time but users judge the wait by TTFT and steady flow. SSE format: lines data: <payload> separated by a blank line, content type text/event-stream.

Checklist: disable proxy buffering (for nginx, X-Accel-Buffering: no or proxy_buffering off); heartbeat comments to keep idle connections alive; bound server-side buffers and cancel generation when the client disconnects (otherwise the GPU keeps working for nobody); mark partial results as incomplete; support resume with an event ID or a fresh request; apply output filters incrementally or hold back risky segments; on Android, read the stream with OkHttp and update UI state in batches, not one recomposition per token.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
(server endpoint streaming SSE)

# FastAPI sketch; token_stream() is your async generator of text pieces
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/chat")
async def chat(q: str):
    async def events():
        async for tok in token_stream(q):
            yield f"data: {tok}\n\n"
        yield "event: done\ndata: {}\n\n"
    return StreamingResponse(events(), media_type="text/event-stream",
                             headers={"X-Accel-Buffering": "no", "Cache-Control": "no-cache"})
// Spring WebFlux; tokenFlux(q) returns Flux<String> (assumed helper)
@GetMapping("/chat", produces = [MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE])
fun chat(@RequestParam q: String): Flux<ServerSentEvent<String>> =
    tokenFlux(q).map { ServerSentEvent.builder(it).build() }
// Spring WebFlux; tokenFlux(q) returns Flux<String> (assumed helper)
@GetMapping(value = "/chat", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
public Flux<ServerSentEvent<String>> chat(@RequestParam String q) {
    return tokenFlux(q).map(t -> ServerSentEvent.builder(t).build());
}

sections.html:
• Streaming through a gzip or buffering proxy and seeing all text arrive at once.
  • Continuing generation after the client disconnects.
  • Saving a partial answer as final.

sections.html:
1. SSE vs WebSocket? → SSE is simpler, one-way, auto-reconnect; WebSocket is two-way, better for cancel/interrupt.
  2. How handle a slow client? → Bounded buffer; drop connection or coalesce tokens.
  3. Moderation on streams? → Incremental checks with a short lookahead window or post-hoc retraction.

questions.promptHtml: What is prefill/decode disaggregation, what does it buy you, and when would you not do it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A senior design trade-off question: complexity versus SLO control.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Run prefill on one pool of GPUs and decode on another, transferring the KV cache between them. Each pool can be sized, parallelized and tuned for its own bottleneck, so a heavy prefill never stalls decode and you can hit strict TTFT and TPOT SLOs together. The costs are KV transfer latency and bandwidth, extra operational complexity, and wasted capacity if the pool ratio is wrong. For modest loads, chunked prefill is usually enough.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Prefill pool: compute-bound, favours high tensor parallelism and large token batches to minimize TTFT. Decode pool: memory-bound, favours large batches with big KV memory to maximize tokens per second at a TPOT SLO.

Transfer cost example: a 4k-token prompt on a 128 KiB/token model is 512 MiB of KV. Over a 50 GB/s link that is ~10 ms; over a slow 1 GB/s network it is ~0.5 s, which would wreck TTFT. So it needs fast interconnect (NVLink, InfiniBand/RDMA) or short prompts.

Pool sizing: choose the prefill:decode ratio from the prompt/output token mix; the ratio shifts with traffic, so autoscale each independently. Skip when prompts are short, traffic small, or interconnect slow.

• Ignoring transfer time and cache-locality loss (prefix caches now live on prefill nodes).
  • Static pool ratios that drift out of balance.

1. Alternative with less complexity? → Chunked prefill with a decode-first budget.
  2. What fails over? → Decode node loss means recompute or reload the KV; design for it.
  3. Which metric improves most? → p99 TPOT/inter-token stability, plus independent TTFT control.

questions.subtopic: When speculative decoding stops paying off
questions.promptHtml: Under what conditions does speculative decoding give no benefit or make things worse? Show it with numbers.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who deploy optimizations by checklist from those who understand their cost model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It pays only if the expected accepted tokens per round exceed the extra cost of drafting. That fails when acceptance is low (creative text, high temperature, poorly matched draft) or when the system is already compute-bound at large batch sizes, where verifying extra tokens uses real compute that other requests would have used.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Speed-up S = E[tokens] / (1 + gamma c), E = (1 - alpha^(gamma+1)) / (1 - alpha), c = draft/target cost ratio. With gamma 4, c 0.1 (overhead 1.4):

alpha E[tokens] S
0.8 3.36 ~2.4x
0.5 1.94 ~1.4x
0.3 1.42 ~1.0x

Batch effect: at low concurrency spare compute makes verification nearly free. At batch 64+ the GPU has little spare compute, the verification of rejected tokens becomes wasted work, and throughput can drop below baseline even if per-request latency looks better. Also memory: the draft model and its cache reduce KV capacity, shrinking max batch.

Decision procedure: measure acceptance on production-like prompts, A/B at realistic concurrency, and enable per route (for example only on low-load or code-heavy routes), or switch it off dynamically under load.

sections.html:
• Benchmarking at batch 1 and deploying at batch 64.
  • Using a draft from a different tokenizer or a badly distilled one.
  • Judging by a toy prompt with high acceptance.

sections.html:
1. Raise gamma? → More tokens per round only if alpha is high; otherwise more waste.
  2. Cheaper drafting? → n-gram/prompt lookup or Medusa/EAGLE heads, no second model.
  3. Output distribution still correct when it hurts speed? → Yes, correctness is independent of acceptance.

questions.contextHtml: Your chat service runs on 6 replicas of an 8B model with continuous batching. Dashboards: p50 TTFT 350 ms, p50 TPOT 35 ms. Since Monday, p99 inter-token latency jumps from 60 ms to 1.8 s in bursts and users report "freezing" mid-answer. The release notes show a new "upload a PDF and chat" feature; prompts of 40k to 60k tokens now make up ~3% of traffic. GPU utilization is steady at 85%. Average latency looks fine. Network and client code did not change.
questions.promptHtml: How do you diagnose and fix this?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more GPUs" or "lower the batch size". More replicas do not remove the stall, and lowering batch size cuts throughput while barely touching the cause.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do freezes correlate with long-prompt arrivals (timestamps)? Is chunked prefill on? What are max batched tokens and max sequences? Are long requests routed to the same pool as chat? What is the SLO on inter-token latency?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap prompt length at the edge temporarily or route long-document requests to a dedicated replica (1 of 6) so the other 5 keep smooth decode.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Un-chunked 50k-token prefill monopolizes each step. (b) KV pressure triggers preemptions. (c) Network/proxy hiccups (red herring, since stalls align with server step time). (d) GC or CPU contention on the API tier.
  4. How I'd verify each: Plot inter-token latency histograms against prompt-length arrivals; read engine metrics for step time and preemption counters; trace one frozen request; check whether the stall duration matches prefill time (50k tokens at ~25k tokens/s is ~2 s).
  5. Root cause: A 50k-token prefill makes a single step last ~2 s, and every running sequence waits for that step to finish.
  6. Fix: Short term, enable chunked prefill with a token budget of about 2,048 per step and prioritize decode tokens. Long term, isolate document traffic in its own pool or add disaggregation, and cache the document prefix so follow-up questions skip prefill.
  7. Prevention: Alert on p99 ITL, not mean TPOT; load-test with a realistic length mix including the 3% long tail; admission limits by tokens, not requests.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Chunking raises the long request's TTFT by a few seconds; acceptable for documents. I would not shrink the global batch, and I would not trust averages.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Long prompts rise to 15% of traffic? → Dedicated prefill capacity or disaggregation becomes worth the complexity.
  • Users chat with the same PDF repeatedly? → Prefix caching makes later turns cheap; route sticky by document.
  • Chunked prefill enabled but stalls persist? → Check the budget size, and whether the scheduler prioritizes decode first.

sections.html: A team blamed the network for months of "random freezes"; one histogram of step durations lined up perfectly with large uploads, and a single flag removed the complaints.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales hardware or lowers batch size without evidence.
  • Hire: identifies prefill interference and enables chunked prefill.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the stall, isolates traffic classes, adds prefix caching and tail-based alerts.

questions.contextHtml:
A support-chat backend streams answers. Users on the corporate VPN report the answer appears all at once after ~15 s; users on mobile say that after a flaky connection they sometimes see half answers in their history that look "complete". Server code:

@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(req: Req):
    async def gen():
        text = ""
        try:
            async for tok in llm_stream(req.prompt):
                text += tok
                yield tok
        finally:
            db.save_message(req.user, text)      # persist the answer
    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/plain")

Traffic passes through a corporate proxy and an nginx ingress with default settings.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Streaming is slow on VPN, increase the timeout." Misses both bugs: proxy buffering and the unconditional save.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the delay happen only behind the proxy? Does a direct curl to the backend stream properly? Is generation cancelled when clients disconnect? Are messages versioned or flagged?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add X-Accel-Buffering: no and disable proxy buffering for this route; stop saving in finally and mark partials.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Response buffering in nginx or proxy (all text delivered at once). (b) finally runs on client disconnect too, saving partial text as complete. (c) text/plain without SSE framing makes some proxies buffer more. (d) LLM slow (red herring: curl direct shows steady tokens).
  4. How I'd verify each: curl -N against the pod, then against the ingress, comparing arrival times; simulate a disconnect and inspect the DB row.
  5. Root cause: Intermediary buffering plus a persistence path that cannot tell completion from cancellation.
  6. Fix:
@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(req: Req):
    async def gen():
        text, done = "", False
        try:
            async for tok in llm_stream(req.prompt):
                text += tok
                yield f"data: {tok}\n\n"
            done = True
            yield "event: done\ndata: {}\n\n"
        finally:
            db.save_message(req.user, text, status="complete" if done else "partial")
    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream",
                             headers={"X-Accel-Buffering": "no", "Cache-Control": "no-cache"})
// Spring: flag completion in doOnComplete, partial in doOnCancel
tokenFlux(q)
    .doOnComplete { repo.save(user, text, "complete") }
    .doOnCancel { repo.save(user, text, "partial") }
tokenFlux(q)
    .doOnComplete(() -> repo.save(user, text, "complete"))
    .doOnCancel(() -> repo.save(user, text, "partial"));
  1. Prevention: An integration test that streams through the real ingress; test for disconnect behaviour; track "cancelled" generations so GPU work stops.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not drop the save (users want history); do not disable buffering globally, only for streaming routes.

• Client reconnects mid-answer? → Event IDs and a resume endpoint, or regenerate; never splice blindly.

  • Gzip on? → It buffers; exclude event-stream.

  • Hire: finds buffering and the partial-save bug.
  • Strong hire: also cancels upstream generation, adds SSE framing and an ingress-level test.

Benchmarks on one GPU replica with an 8B fp16 model: 3,000 output tokens/s at the SLO, 128 KiB of KV per token, 56 GB free for KV. Product wants "N+1 and a bit of headroom". The CFO asks how many GPUs.
questions.promptHtml: Size the fleet and justify it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Divide total requests by a vague "requests per GPU" figure, ignoring percentiles, memory and redundancy.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 30 req/s the true peak or hourly average? How much prefix reuse? Are there long-document users? Is a hosted API an acceptable overflow?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (planning); I would start from a pilot at lower scale.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Output tokens/s is the main constraint; KV memory limits concurrency; prefill rate affects TTFT.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay recorded traffic with a load generator at the target mix and measure tokens/s at the SLO; check memory fit.
  5. Root cause / computation: Output demand = 30 x 500 = 15,000 tokens/s. At 3,000 per replica that is 5. Add 25% headroom: 6.25, so 7. Add N+1: 8 replicas. Concurrency by Little's law: each request lasts about 0.5 s + 500 x 0.04 s = 20.5 s; in flight = 30 x 20.5 = ~615 across 8 replicas, ~77 each. KV: 77 x (2,000+500 tokens) x 128 KiB = ~24 GB < 56 GB, fine; at p95 lengths (4,400 tokens) ~43 GB, still fits. Prefill load is 60,000 tokens/s, so verify prefill stays within the TTFT SLO in the benchmark, not just output rate.
  6. Fix / plan: 8 replicas across zones, autoscale on queue depth and KV usage, with warm pool, prefix caching to reduce prefill.
  7. Prevention: Re-forecast monthly; alert at 70% sustained utilization.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not size on average rate; do not skip the N+1; consider fp8 KV or a smaller model to cut cost after quality evals.

• Peak doubles on launch? → 16 replicas or overflow to a hosted API plus load shedding.
  • Outputs average 1,000 tokens? → Demand doubles; replicas ~14.
  • One zone dies? → N+1 must be per-zone: lose a zone, still meet peak, so budget extra.

questions.contextHtml: A vLLM-style server hosts a 70B model on 4 GPUs (tensor parallel). After a launch, a longer system prompt raises average context from 3k to 9k tokens. Symptoms: throughput falls 40%, p99 TTFT climbs from 1.2 s to 9 s, and logs show preempted request ... recompute several hundred times per minute. GPU utilization is 95% but useful tokens/s is down. Memory utilization setting is 0.90. Nothing else changed.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "GPU is at 95%, so we are at capacity, buy more." Misses that utilization is wasted on recomputation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What are max sequences and max model length? Cache hit rate? Preemption mode (swap vs recompute)? Current concurrency? Is the longer prompt shared across users?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce max concurrent sequences or the max model length to stop thrashing; roll back the prompt if it is the sole cause.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) KV cache exhausted: 3x longer contexts mean 3x less concurrency fits, the scheduler admits more than memory supports, then preempts and recomputes. (b) Prefix cache evicted too early. (c) Network issues (red herring: preemption counters point to memory). (d) Cache fragmentation (unlikely with paging).
  4. How I'd verify each: Engine metrics for KV usage percent, preemption count, prefix cache hit rate; compute KV bytes/token x tokens x sequences against free memory.
  5. Root cause: Demand for KV memory outgrew supply; each preemption throws away prefill work and re-queues it, creating a death spiral where compute is spent on redo.
  6. Fix: Short term: cap concurrency to fit KV and let excess requests queue or be shed. Enable prefix caching so the shared 6k-token preamble is stored once (copy-on-write sharing). Use fp8 KV cache (2x capacity) after an eval. Long term: shrink the system prompt, use a GQA/MLA model, add replicas or CPU offload for cold prefixes.
  7. Prevention: Alerts on preemption rate and KV usage above ~85%; capacity tests with the new context distribution before changing prompts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not raise memory utilization to 0.99 (risks OOM from activations); do not rely on swapping to CPU over slow PCIe at high rates.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Prefix caching on, hit rate only 10%? → Variable content early in the prompt; reorder.
  • fp8 KV accuracy worry? → Run the eval suite and compare; roll out by canary.
  • Mixed lengths? → Use separate pools for long-context traffic.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "harmless" prompt rewrite tripled context and halved capacity; the fix was moving the dynamic part to the end so one cached copy served all users.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds GPUs.
  • Hire: ties preemptions to KV exhaustion and caps concurrency.
  • Strong hire: quantifies memory, uses prefix sharing and fp8, adds preemption alerts and pooled routing.

questions.contextHtml: You enabled speculative decoding (draft model, 5 tokens) on a 34B model. A single-user benchmark shows 2.2x faster decode. In production at peak (batch around 80), throughput drops from 6,000 to 5,100 tokens/s and p95 TPOT is unchanged. Off-peak (batch 6) users report responses feel twice as fast. Acceptance rate averages 0.72 for chat and 0.35 for creative-writing tenants. The team wants a decision before the next release.
questions.promptHtml: Keep it, remove it, or change it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "It works in the benchmark, so keep it on" or "it's broken, remove it".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the latency SLO versus the cost goal? How is traffic split by tenant? How much memory does the draft take from the KV pool? What are the draft and target costs?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable speculation above a load threshold (queue depth or batch size) and for creative tenants.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) At batch 80 the GPU is compute-bound, so verifying rejected draft tokens steals compute. (b) Low acceptance for creative text (alpha 0.35 gives about 1.5 tokens per round for 6 tokens verified). (c) Draft weights and cache reduce KV capacity, lowering max batch.
  4. How I'd verify each: A/B at fixed concurrency levels (1, 8, 32, 80) with and without speculation; per-tenant acceptance logging; KV capacity before/after.
  5. Root cause: The optimization trades spare compute for latency; at peak there is no spare compute.
  6. Fix: Load-aware policy: enable at low concurrency and for high-acceptance routes; keep off at peak; consider n-gram or prompt-lookup speculation for extraction workloads, which needs no draft model memory. Compute: alpha 0.72, gamma 5 gives (1-0.72^6)/0.28 = ~3.2 tokens per round.
  7. Prevention: Benchmark matrices across batch sizes and tenants; dashboards for acceptance rate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not set one global flag; do not accept reduced peak throughput silently because it requires buying more GPUs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Leadership wants lower cost, not latency? → Remove it at peak; it only helps latency.
  • Draft model retrained? → Acceptance may rise; re-measure per tenant.
  • Using EAGLE-style heads? → No second model memory, still same compute argument.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A flag that sped up demos cost an extra replica at peak; a threshold on queue depth saved both the experience and the budget.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: all-or-nothing decision.
  • Hire: explains compute-bound vs memory-bound regimes.
  • Strong hire: load-aware, tenant-aware policy backed by A/B data and memory impact.

questions.contextHtml:
A RAG agent sends this on every call (system prompt about 3,200 tokens). Prefix caching is enabled on the server, yet the cache hit rate is 0.4% and TTFT p50 is 1.1 s. Cost reports show the full price on all input tokens of the hosted-API fallback too.

def build_messages(question, docs, user):
    system = f"""You are SupportBot. Current time: {datetime.utcnow().isoformat()}
User: {user.name} (id {user.id})
{TOOL_DEFINITIONS_JSON}
{FEW_SHOT_EXAMPLES}"""
    return [{"role": "system", "content": system},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"{docs}\n\nQ: {question}"}]

TOOL_DEFINITIONS_JSON is built by json.dumps(tools) from a set, so the key order varies between processes.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the cache missing and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase cache size." The problem is the prefix content, not capacity.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How is the hit rate measured? How many replicas, and is routing sticky? Does the hosted API report cached tokens? How long is the TTL relative to the request gap?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move dynamic fields out of the prefix right now; sort tool definitions.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Timestamp in the first line changes every call so no block matches. (b) User name/id before the static content. (c) Non-deterministic tool ordering across processes. (d) Round-robin routing across replicas (secondary). (e) Eviction (red herring at 0.4%).
  4. How I'd verify each: Hash the first 3,200 tokens of two consecutive requests and diff; check the response usage field for cached token counts; look at the per-replica hit rate.
  5. Root cause: The KV of every token depends on all earlier tokens, so a changed first line invalidates the whole prompt.
  6. Fix:
STATIC = SYSTEM_RULES + json.dumps(tools, sort_keys=True) + FEW_SHOT_EXAMPLES  # built once
def build_messages(question, docs, user):
    return [{"role": "system", "content": STATIC},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Now: {now_iso()} | User: {user.name}\n{docs}\n\nQ: {question}"}]
val STATIC = SYSTEM_RULES + mapper.writer().writeValueAsString(sortedTools) + FEW_SHOT // built once
fun buildMessages(q: String, docs: String, user: User) = listOf(
    Msg("system", STATIC),
    Msg("user", "Now: ${Instant.now()} | User: ${user.name}\n$docs\n\nQ: $q"))
static final String STATIC = SYSTEM_RULES + mapper.writeValueAsString(sortedTools) + FEW_SHOT; // built once
List<Msg> buildMessages(String q, String docs, User user) {
    return List.of(new Msg("system", STATIC),
        new Msg("user", "Now: " + Instant.now() + " | User: " + user.name() + "\n" + docs + "\n\nQ: " + q));
}
  1. Prevention: A unit test asserting the prefix is byte-identical across calls; hit-rate and cached-token dashboards; a lint rule banning dynamic values in system prompts.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Dynamic content must still reach the model (just later); do not hide the user's identity from the model if it truly needs it; use sticky routing by conversation if replicas are many.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The model needs the time early? → Put it right after the static block, before the user content.
  • Hosted API caching has a TTL? → Keep traffic regular or accept misses on idle prefixes; verify TTL in docs.
  • Expected savings? → 3,200 of ~4,500 tokens skip prefill; TTFT drops about 70% of prefill time.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single timestamp in the first line cost a team a six-figure yearly token bill; moving it to the end dropped input costs by two thirds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks cache size.
  • Hire: finds the timestamp and reorders content.
  • Strong hire: also finds nondeterministic serialization, adds tests, routing and monitoring.

questions.contextHtml: Marketing launches a campaign expected to increase traffic from 5 to 50 requests/s within 10 minutes. Replicas are 4 GPUs each running a 70B model; loading weights from object storage takes 6 minutes, and your autoscaler scales on average GPU utilization with a 5-minute window. Last spike: queue wait went from 0.2 s to 45 s, clients timed out at 30 s, retries doubled the load, and the system oscillated for an hour.
questions.promptHtml: How do you make this launch survive?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set the autoscaler more aggressively." Cold start of 6 minutes beats any threshold tuning; no mention of shedding or retries.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Hard peak and duration? Priorities between users? Is a hosted fallback allowed? Can I pre-provision for the event? What do clients do on timeout?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pre-scale before launch to the forecast (planned, not reactive); enable admission control with a queue-time limit (reject with 429 and Retry-After at 5 s queue); disable aggressive client retries.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Slow cold start plus a lagging metric. (b) Retry storms amplify the load. (c) Average GPU utilization hides saturation, since decode can show 100% with growing queues. (d) Stale health checks routing to loading replicas.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay the previous spike's metrics; load test with the 10x ramp; measure load time breakdown (download vs init vs warm-up).
  5. Root cause: A reactive control loop slower than the traffic ramp, no admission control, retries without backoff.
  6. Fix: Scale on queue depth and KV usage with short windows; keep a warm pool (a few ready replicas); cache weights on local NVMe or a pre-baked image to cut load to ~1 to 2 minutes; readiness probe only after warm-up request; client backoff with jitter; fallback to a smaller model or hosted API when queue exceeds the limit; priority classes so paid users go first.
  7. Prevention: Game-day load tests; runbook for planned events; SLO burn-rate alerts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Warm pools cost money idle; I would pay it only before known events. Do not let queues grow unbounded (it turns latency into outage).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cannot get 40 more GPUs in time? → Shed low-priority load, route to a smaller model, enable fp8 and longer batching for throughput.
  • Traffic is bursty not planned? → Keep headroom (N+2) and a hosted overflow.
  • Why queue depth over GPU utilization? → It leads the problem; utilization saturates early and stays flat.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch survived only because the team had set a 5-second queue-time reject rule; the previous event had melted down through retries.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: lowers the autoscaler threshold.
  • Hire: pre-scales and adds admission control.
  • Strong hire: combines leading metrics, fast weights loading, retry discipline, fallback and priorities.

questions.contextHtml: Two products share one inference fleet of 12 GPUs. Product A (interactive chat) needs p95 TTFT under 800 ms and TPOT under 40 ms. Product B (nightly batch summarization, 2 million documents of 6k tokens each, 300-token outputs) needs completion within 8 hours. Today both run with the same settings (max 128 sequences, no priorities) and chat p95 TTFT is 3 s during the night run. Finance wants fewer GPUs.
questions.promptHtml: How do you reconfigure and what is the minimum GPU count you can defend?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run both on the same cluster and hope the scheduler sorts it out," or "Give B its own GPUs without computing the need."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Chat peak vs off-peak load? Is B's deadline hard? Can B run in the day's quiet hours? Same model for both? Is prefix caching applicable to B (shared instructions)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Put B at lowest priority with a capped share of tokens per step, or throttle it, so chat TTFT recovers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: B's long prefills (6k tokens) crowd the step budget and queue; chat shares queue and batch limits; no preemption of batch work.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run chat-only and mixed benchmarks and compare TTFT; measure per-replica throughput of B alone.
  5. Root cause / computation: B total input = 2M x 6k = 12B prefill tokens plus 600M output tokens in 8 h (28,800 s): 417k prefill tokens/s and 20.8k output tokens/s. If a replica handles ~25k prefill tokens/s at big batch and ~3,000 output tokens/s, B alone needs ~17 replicas for prefill alone: more than the fleet, so the deadline needs checking (verify with real benchmarks, since prefill and decode share the same GPU time). Options: extend the deadline, trim input, use prefix caching for shared instructions, a smaller model, or run during chat's quiet hours (which the 8 hour night window already is).
  6. Fix: Priority scheduling (chat first), a separate batch pool or time-sliced allocation at night, large batch size and large chunk for B (throughput mode) and small, latency-tuned settings for A; scale chat down at night and give freed GPUs to B; use hosted batch APIs for overflow.
  7. Prevention: SLO per class, dashboards for goodput by class, a capacity model refreshed monthly.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not tune a single config for both; do not accept B's deadline without the arithmetic; cutting GPUs further would break one of the two SLOs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• B deadline relaxes to 24 h? → Tokens/s needed drops 3x, and the fleet suffices.
  • Chat doubles? → Separate pools become necessary, B moves to spot or hosted batch capacity.
  • Quantizing B to int4/fp8? → More throughput; validate quality on the summarization eval.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A nightly job quietly consumed day capacity because its start slipped; priority classes and a hard time-window turned a recurring incident into a non-event.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: gives a GPU count with no math.
  • Hire: separates classes with priorities and computes B's token needs.
  • Strong hire: finds that the deadline is infeasible as stated, proposes levers (deadline, prefix cache, smaller model, hosted batch) with numbers.
